The clean answer is to avoid server-side state: issue a signed token such as a JWT, keep the state on the client, and let every instance verify it independently. When sessions are unavoidable, for example a legacy server-rendered app, Spring Session moves the session out of memory into Redis: spring-session-data-redis replaces the HttpSession implementation, every instance reads the same store, and the application becomes horizontally scalable. The trade-offs are a new dependency on Redis availability and the need to keep session contents small and serializable. Session fixation and timeout settings belong in the security configuration, not in application code.
followUps: Why are sticky sessions a bad long-term answer?
What breaks if you store a non-serializable object in a Spring Session?
question: How do you handle sessions in a Spring Boot application that runs on several instances?
shortAnswer: Prefer stateless authentication with tokens so there is no session to share; if you must keep server-side sessions, externalise them with Spring Session backed by Redis so any instance can serve any request.
tips: Recommend stateless first, then Spring Session as the fallback.
Mention Redis as the shared store.
title: Session management and clustering in Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Buffering without a bound.
Dropping items from a stream where loss is unacceptable.
detailedAnswer: In a blocking world, a slow consumer simply blocks the producer's thread. In a reactive pipeline there are no blocked threads, so the problem becomes explicit: a fast publisher can overwhelm a slow subscriber. The Reactive Streams specification solves this with demand: the subscriber requests N items, and the publisher must not send more than requested. Reactor builds on this with operators: onBackpressureBuffer queues excess items, which is safe only with a bound, because an unbounded buffer is just an out-of-memory error waiting to happen; onBackpressureDrop discards items the consumer cannot keep up with, which fits metrics and telemetry; onBackpressureLatest keeps only the newest item, which fits live dashboards. The design lesson is to choose the strategy from the data: financial transactions must never be dropped, so they need buffering plus a slow producer, while a sensor feed can drop. This is different from executor backpressure, which uses bounded queues and rejection policies on thread pools.
followUps: Which backpressure strategy fits a payment stream, and which fits a sensor feed?
Why is an unbounded buffer the worst option?
question: What is backpressure in reactive streams, and how do you handle a fast producer and a slow consumer?
shortAnswer: Backpressure is the consumer telling the producer how much it can handle, using demand signals; in Reactor you handle overload with strategies such as buffering, dropping, or keeping only the latest item, and the worst choice is an unbounded buffer.
tips: Explain demand first: the consumer sets the pace.
Contrast with executor backpressure to show the distinction.
title: Backpressure in reactive streams

commonMistakes: Returning false for null inside a custom validator.
Writing validation logic in the controller instead of a constraint.
detailedAnswer: Built-in constraints such as @NotNull and @Size cover the common cases, but business rules need custom ones, for example a discount code that must match a pattern and exist in the catalogue. The recipe has three parts: an annotation that declares the message, groups, and payload and is meta-annotated with @Constraint(validatedBy = ...); a validator class implementing ConstraintValidator<YourAnnotation, String> whose isValid method returns false for bad values and true for null, because null is @NotNull's job; and the annotation placed on the DTO field. Spring Boot runs validation automatically when a controller parameter is annotated with @Valid, and failures arrive as a MethodArgumentNotValidException that a @ControllerAdvice turns into a 400 with field-level errors. A validator can also be a Spring bean, so it can inject a repository to check the value against the database, which is how existence checks are done.
followUps: Should isValid return true or false for null?
How do you validate a value against the database?
question: How do you write a custom validation annotation in Spring Boot?
shortAnswer: Define an annotation meta-annotated with @Constraint(validatedBy = YourValidator.class), implement ConstraintValidator with the isValid logic, and place the annotation on the field; Spring validates it automatically when the object is bound with @Valid.
tips: Give the three-part recipe in order.
Mention that null is @NotNull's job, not the validator's.
title: Custom Bean Validation in Spring Boot

commonMistakes: Assuming a checked exception rolls back by default.
Raising isolation to SERIALIZABLE everywhere.
detailedAnswer: Propagation answers 'which transaction am I in?' REQUIRED, the default, joins the existing transaction or starts one if there is none, so the whole call stack commits or rolls back together. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the caller's transaction, starts a new one, and commits it independently, which is exactly what an audit log needs: the audit row must survive even if the business operation rolls back. NESTED runs inside the caller's transaction with a savepoint, so it can roll back alone. Isolation answers 'what can I see?': READ_COMMITTED sees only committed data, REPEATABLE_READ re-reads the same rows consistently, and SERIALIZABLE is fully isolated but slow. The default isolation comes from the database, and raising it is a performance cost, not a free correctness win. Two practical rules: only unchecked exceptions trigger rollback by default, so a checked exception needs rollbackFor, and @Transactional on a method only works when the call goes through the Spring proxy, so self-invocation silently runs without a transaction.
followUps: Why would audit logging use REQUIRES_NEW?
Why does calling a @Transactional method from inside the same class not start a transaction?
question: What do transaction propagation and isolation control, and when would you use REQUIRES_NEW?
shortAnswer: Propagation decides whether a method joins the caller's transaction or starts its own, and isolation decides how much concurrent transactions can see of each other. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the caller's transaction and starts a fresh one, which is how you make audit logging survive a rollback.
tips: Use the audit-log example for REQUIRES_NEW; it is the canonical case.
Mention the unchecked-exception rollback rule.
title: Transaction propagation and isolation in Spring

commonMistakes: Returning entities directly from controllers.
Setting only one side of the relationship.
detailedAnswer: A bidirectional relationship means the parent holds a list of children and each child holds a reference back to the parent. Jackson follows references naively, so serialising the parent writes the children, each child writes the parent, and the cycle never ends until a StackOverflowError. The quick fixes are Jackson annotations: @JsonManagedReference on the parent side and @JsonBackReference on the child side tells Jackson to serialise the forward direction only, and @JsonIgnore simply drops the back reference. The better fix is architectural: do not return entities from controllers at all. Map to a DTO that contains exactly the fields the API promises, which also stops lazy-loading surprises and accidental data exposure. Two related rules: the owning side of the relationship is the one without mappedBy, and you should always set both sides of the relationship in code, using a helper method, or the in-memory object graph will disagree with the database.
followUps: Which side of a bidirectional relationship owns it, and how do you tell?
Why is returning a DTO better than a Jackson annotation here?
question: Why does returning a bidirectional JPA entity as JSON cause infinite recursion, and how do you fix it?
shortAnswer: Because the parent serialises its children and each child serialises its parent, forever. Fix it with @JsonManagedReference and @JsonBackReference, with @JsonIgnore, or, preferably, by returning a DTO instead of the entity.
tips: Explain the cycle first, then give the quick fix and the right fix.
Mention the helper method for keeping both sides in sync.
title: Bidirectional JPA relationships and infinite JSON recursion

commonMistakes: Enabling the second-level cache without an invalidation plan.
Expecting it to cache query results automatically.
detailedAnswer: Every Session has a first-level cache: within one session, loading the same entity twice returns the same object and no second query runs. The second-level cache extends that across sessions and across the application, so a second request for the same entity can skip the database entirely. It is configured per entity with @Cacheable and a cache concurrency strategy, and it needs a provider such as Ehcache or Hazelcast. It shines for reference data that is read constantly and changes rarely, such as countries or product categories. It hurts when the data changes often, because every write must invalidate the cached copy, and a stale cache is a correctness bug, not a performance problem. It also does nothing for queries: query results need the query cache enabled separately, and it is invalidated aggressively. The rule is to measure first, cache reference data only, and treat invalidation as part of the design.
followUps: What is the difference between the first and second level caches?
Why is caching write-heavy data usually a mistake?
question: What is the Hibernate second-level cache, and when does it hurt more than it helps?
shortAnswer: The first-level cache is the persistence context, scoped to one session; the second-level cache is shared across sessions, backed by a provider such as Ehcache, and it helps read-heavy, rarely changing data while hurting write-heavy or frequently invalidated data.
tips: Contrast the two caches by scope first.
Name the fit: read-heavy reference data.
title: Hibernate second-level cache

commonMistakes: Adding indexes without ever reading a plan.
Trusting the estimated row counts without ANALYZE.
detailedAnswer: Guessing about performance is a waste of time; the plan is the evidence. EXPLAIN shows the execution plan the database chose, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and adds real timings. The things to look for are a sequential scan on a large table where an index should apply, which usually means the index is missing or the predicate does not match it; a large gap between estimated and actual rows, which means the statistics are stale and ANALYZE is needed; and nested loops over large inputs, which suggest a missing join index. The common reasons an index is ignored are a function wrapped around the indexed column, a type mismatch that prevents the comparison, or a query that returns most of the table, where a scan is genuinely cheaper. The workflow is: reproduce the slow query, read the plan, fix the cause, and re-run the plan to confirm the change.
followUps: Why would a database ignore an existing index?
What does a big gap between estimated and actual rows mean?
question: How do you use EXPLAIN to find out why a query is slow?
shortAnswer: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query and read the plan: look for sequential scans on large tables, check the estimated versus actual row counts, and confirm the index you expect is actually being used.
tips: Describe the workflow: reproduce, read the plan, fix, confirm.
Name the function-on-indexed-column trap.
title: Using EXPLAIN to check whether a query uses an index

commonMistakes: Retrying against a service that is already down.
Returning an error as the fallback instead of a degraded answer.
detailedAnswer: A retry alone makes a failing dependency worse, because every client keeps hammering it. A circuit breaker stops the bleeding. In the closed state, calls pass through and the breaker counts failures; when the failure rate crosses a threshold over a window, it trips to open, and calls fail immediately with a fallback instead of waiting for a timeout. That fail-fast behaviour protects both sides: the caller gets a quick answer and the struggling service gets time to recover. After a configured wait, the breaker moves to half-open and allows a small number of trial calls; if they succeed, it closes and normal traffic resumes, and if they fail, it opens again. The tuning parameters are the failure threshold, the window, and the open-state duration, and the fallback must be a real degradation, such as cached data or a default, not an exception disguised as a response. Resilience4j is the usual implementation in Spring Boot, and it composes with retry and bulkhead.
followUps: How is a Circuit Breaker different from a Retry?
What should a fallback return?
question: How does a Circuit Breaker actually work, and what are its three states?
shortAnswer: Closed means calls flow normally while failures are counted; when failures pass a threshold the breaker opens and calls fail fast without reaching the service; after a timeout it goes half-open, letting a few trial calls through to test recovery before closing again.
tips: Walk the three states in order; interviewers ask for them by name.
Stress fail-fast as the point of the pattern.
title: Circuit Breaker states: closed, open, and half-open

commonMistakes: Hardcoding service addresses in configuration.
Assuming client-side caching is always fresh.
detailedAnswer: Both solve the same problem: service addresses change as instances start and stop, so callers cannot hardcode them. With client-side discovery, the calling service queries the registry, caches the instance list, and chooses one, usually with a client-side load balancer. That gives the client control over load-balancing and failover, but every client needs registry logic and a cache. With server-side discovery, the client calls a fixed address, a load balancer or a Kubernetes Service, and that component resolves the instance. The client is simpler and needs no registry knowledge, but the load balancer is another component to run and a potential bottleneck. In practice, Kubernetes users get server-side discovery from Services almost for free, while Spring Cloud users historically used client-side discovery with Eureka; modern service meshes move the logic into a sidecar proxy, which is effectively server-side discovery per instance.
followUps: Which model does a Kubernetes Service use?
What is the downside of putting discovery logic in every client?
question: What is the difference between client-side and server-side service discovery?
shortAnswer: In client-side discovery the client asks the registry and picks an instance itself, as with Eureka and a client load balancer; in server-side discovery the client calls a load balancer, which asks the registry and forwards the request, as with a cloud load balancer or Kubernetes Service.
tips: Frame it as: who picks the instance, the caller or a middleman?
Mention the service mesh as the modern convergence.
title: Client-side versus server-side service discovery

commonMistakes: Adopting a mesh for five services.
Assuming a mesh removes the need for application-level resilience.
detailedAnswer: In a plain microservices system, every service reimplements the same concerns: encrypting traffic, retrying failures, emitting metrics, and routing canary traffic. A service mesh extracts all of that into a proxy, usually Envoy, injected as a sidecar container next to each service; application code makes plain calls to localhost, and the proxy handles the rest. The control plane, such as Istio or Linkerd, configures all the proxies centrally, so you can enable mutual TLS everywhere, split traffic for a canary release, or enforce a retry policy without changing any service. The cost is real: another layer to operate, more resource usage per pod, and a new set of failure modes to understand. The honest answer is that a mesh pays off when you have dozens of services and a platform team to run it, and it is unnecessary complexity for a small system where a gateway and good libraries are enough.
followUps: What does the sidecar proxy actually do for a service?
When would you not adopt a service mesh?
question: What is a service mesh, and when would you adopt one?
shortAnswer: A service mesh moves cross-cutting concerns such as mutual TLS, retries, observability, and traffic splitting out of application code into sidecar proxies next to each service, controlled centrally. It is worth it at scale, and overkill for a handful of services.
tips: Lead with the extraction idea: concerns leave the code.
End with the honest cost-benefit judgement.
title: What is a service mesh, and when is it worth it?

commonMistakes: Using the default groupingBy HashMap and losing the order.
Returning a null or a magic character when nothing repeats.
detailedAnswer:
The counting step needs a map that remembers insertion order, because the answer is the first character in the string whose total count exceeds one, not just any repeated character. Group the characters with Collectors.groupingBy, using a LinkedHashMap supplier and counting downstream, then stream the entries in order and pick the first with a count above one. The result is an Optional, because a string with no repeats has no answer, and returning Optional is honest about that. The whole pipeline is linear time with one map of distinct characters as extra space. Note that groupingBy with a custom map supplier is the detail most candidates miss: the default groupingBy returns a HashMap, which loses the order and can return the wrong character.

```java
public Optional<Character> firstRepeated(String input) {
    return input.chars()
            .mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
            .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
                    Function.identity(),
                    LinkedHashMap::new,
                    Collectors.counting()))
            .entrySet().stream()
            .filter(e -> e.getValue() > 1)
            .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
            .findFirst();
}
```

Mention the alternative: a single pass with a HashSet that returns the first character seen twice is simpler and also linear, but it answers a subtly different question, the first character to repeat while scanning, which for most inputs is the same character.
followUps: Why must the map be a LinkedHashMap here?
Is there a simpler single-pass solution, and what does it change?
question: Given a string, find the first repeated character using Stream functions. What is your approach?
shortAnswer: Count occurrences with a LinkedHashMap built through the stream, preserving first-appearance order, then return the first entry whose count is greater than one; if none exists, return an empty result.
tips: Point out the LinkedHashMap supplier; it is the key detail.
Return Optional instead of a sentinel value.
title: Coding: first repeated character with streams

commonMistakes: Scaling up before knowing what is saturated.
Adding caching before confirming the bottleneck is the database.
detailedAnswer: The order matters, because the wrong first move makes things worse. First, confirm it is a real traffic spike and not a retry storm from a failing downstream, by checking request rates, error rates, and downstream latency together. Second, protect the system: enable rate limiting, shed non-critical work such as recommendations or heavy reports, and scale horizontally if the service is stateless, which is why stateless design matters. Third, find the actual bottleneck instead of guessing: thread pool saturation, database connection exhaustion, a hot endpoint doing an N+1 query, or GC pressure each have different signatures in the metrics. Only then make the structural fix: cache the hot reads, move slow work to a queue, add database read replicas, or break the endpoint apart. After the incident, the follow-ups are autoscaling policies, load tests that reproduce the spike, and alerts on saturation metrics such as thread pool usage and connection pool wait time, so the next spike is caught before users feel it.
followUps: How do you tell a genuine traffic spike from a retry storm?
Which saturation metrics would you alert on?
question: Scenario: your Spring Boot service's traffic suddenly triples and response times climb. What do you do, in order?
shortAnswer: First stabilise: confirm the spike is real, shed non-essential load, and scale out. Then find the bottleneck with metrics and profiling, and only then make structural changes such as caching, async processing, or a queue.
tips: Give the sequence: confirm, protect, diagnose, fix.
Name one metric per bottleneck type.
title: Scenario: handling a sudden traffic spike
When to use @Around advice
question: When would you use @Around advice instead of @Before or @AfterReturning, and what can go wrong with it?
shortAnswer: @Around is the only advice that wraps the call: it can time it, retry it, or replace its result. Forgetting proceed() skips the method; calling it twice runs it twice.
detailedAnswer: @Before and @AfterReturning observe a call; only @Around controls it, because it receives a ProceedingJoinPoint and decides whether and when to call proceed(). That makes it the right tool for timing, retrying, caching a result, or short-circuiting a call. The risks follow from the power: forgetting proceed() means the method never executes and the caller gets whatever the advice returns; calling proceed() twice executes the method twice, which is dangerous for writes; and an @Around advice that swallows exceptions changes the method's contract silently. Prefer the narrower advice types unless you need to control the call.
followUps: How would you write a retry aspect with @Around?
Why is a broad pointcut dangerous?
tips: Give the timing-aspect example, then name the two proceed() mistakes.
Say when you would not use @Around: pure logging belongs in @Before.
commonMistakes: Using @Around for simple logging.
Forgetting that proceed() can throw the method's checked exceptions.

title: Detached entities and merge()
question: An entity is loaded in one transaction, modified after the transaction closes, and passed to merge(). What happens — and which object is managed afterwards?
shortAnswer: merge() copies the detached object's state onto a managed instance and returns it. The object you passed in stays detached; changes to it after the merge are ignored.
detailedAnswer: When the persistence context closes, a managed entity becomes detached: Hibernate stops tracking it, so setter calls change the object but write nothing. merge() takes that detached state, loads or creates the corresponding managed instance, copies the state onto it, and returns the managed instance. The common bug is continuing to use the original reference — it is still detached, so further changes to it are silently lost. persist() is different: it makes a transient object managed, and throws if the object already has an identity.
followUps: How is persist() different from merge()?
Why does dirty checking not need an explicit save?
tips: Stress the return value: merge() returns the managed object; the argument stays detached.
Connect it to the four states: transient, managed, detached, removed.
commonMistakes: Using the passed-in object after merge() as if it were managed.
Calling persist() on a detached entity.

title: StampedLock optimistic reads
question: How does a StampedLock optimistic read work, and what is its main danger?
shortAnswer: You take a stamp without locking, read, then validate(stamp): if a writer changed the data, validation fails and you retry under a read lock. The danger is that StampedLock is not reentrant — re-acquiring it in the same thread deadlocks.
detailedAnswer: StampedLock has three modes: write, read, and optimistic read. tryOptimisticRead() returns a stamp without acquiring any lock, so the read runs fully concurrently; afterwards validate(stamp) checks whether a write happened in between, and if it did, the code falls back to a read lock and re-reads. This is faster than a ReadWriteLock when writes are rare. The trap is reentrancy: unlike synchronized or ReentrantLock, acquiring a read or write lock twice in the same thread deadlocks, so StampedLock suits short, carefully written sections, not general-purpose locking.
followUps: When would ReadWriteLock beat StampedLock?
Why validate instead of just trusting the read?
tips: Explain the retry loop: optimistic read, validate, fall back to a read lock.
Name the non-reentrancy trap explicitly.
commonMistakes: Treating StampedLock as a drop-in replacement for ReentrantLock.
Skipping validation and using a possibly stale read.

title: CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier
question: What is the difference between a CountDownLatch and a CyclicBarrier, and when would you use each?
shortAnswer: A latch is a one-shot countdown that waiting threads observe; a barrier is a reusable rendezvous where all parties wait for each other. Use a latch to wait for completion, a barrier for repeated phases.
detailedAnswer: A CountDownLatch is created with a count; workers call countDown() as they finish and other threads block in await() until the count reaches zero. It cannot be reset — a second round needs a new latch. A CyclicBarrier makes N threads wait at a point until all N arrive, then releases them all together, optionally running a barrier action once; it resets automatically, so it fits repeated phases such as iterations of a parallel computation. A Semaphore is the third shape: permits limiting concurrent access to a resource, rather than coordinating timing.
followUps: What would you use to limit concurrent access to a pool of ten connections?
Can a CountDownLatch be reused?
tips: Answer by coordination shape first, class second.
Add the Semaphore contrast to show the family.
commonMistakes: Saying a latch is reusable.
Using a barrier where a latch would do, or vice versa.

title: Virtual threads and ThreadLocal
question: Why is ThreadLocal dangerous with virtual threads, and what should you use instead?
shortAnswer: ThreadLocal state is per virtual thread, so a million virtual threads can mean a million copies of a value — a memory hazard. Pass context explicitly instead.
detailedAnswer: With platform threads, a ThreadLocal costs one copy per pooled thread — a small, bounded number. Virtual threads are cheap and numerous by design, so the same pattern multiplies the state by the number of live virtual threads, and values can linger as long as the virtual thread does. The replacement is to pass context explicitly as a method argument, or to use scoped values, which are designed for carrying immutable context across virtual threads without per-thread storage.
followUps: What is pinning, and how does it relate?
Would you use a thread pool for virtual threads?
tips: Quantify it: bounded pool versus unbounded virtual threads.
Name scoped values as the intended replacement.
commonMistakes: Treating ThreadLocal as free because virtual threads are cheap.
Using ThreadLocal for request context in a per-request virtual thread server.

title: Resource server JWKS validation
question: How does a resource server validate a JWT without calling the authorization server on every request?
shortAnswer: It verifies the signature against the provider's public keys from the JWKS endpoint, and checks issuer, audience, and expiry locally — the keys are fetched once and cached.
detailedAnswer: A resource server does not ask the authorization server about each token. It fetches the provider's public keys from the JWKS endpoint (published at /.well-known/jwks.json), caches them, and verifies the token's signature, issuer (iss), audience (aud), and expiry (exp) locally. In Spring Boot, setting spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri is enough: Boot discovers the JWKS endpoint from the provider's OpenID configuration and the framework's BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter does the validation before the request reaches a controller. A token with a valid signature but the wrong audience must still be rejected — signature alone is not enough.

title: Access token vs id_token
question: What is the difference between an access token and an id_token, and what goes wrong if you confuse them?
shortAnswer: The access token authorizes API calls; the OIDC id_token identifies the user. Sending an id_token to an API as a Bearer token is wrong — it was not issued for that API.
detailedAnswer: The access token is what a client presents to a resource server: it carries scopes and is accepted as proof that the caller may do something. The id_token is an OpenID Connect JWT that states who the user is (subject, issuer, expiry, and profile claims) for the client that logged them in. An id_token is not an authorization credential for an API: the API cannot validate its audience or scopes, and accepting it would let a token minted for login authorize API access. Keep them separate — id_token for identity at the client, access token for authorization at the API.

title: PACELC trade-offs
question: What does PACELC add to CAP?
shortAnswer: CAP covers the partition case (availability vs consistency); PACELC adds the normal case (latency vs consistency), so the trade-off is made per dataset in both situations.
detailedAnswer: CAP says that during a partition a system chooses availability or consistency. PACELC adds the else: when there is no partition, the system chooses latency or consistency. Strongly consistent reads usually cost a round trip to the leader or a quorum; reading the nearest replica is faster but possibly stale. So a system can be PA/EL (available during partitions, low-latency reads otherwise, like a social feed), PC/EC (consistent in both cases, slower, like a bank ledger), or mixed per dataset — strong consistency for payments, eventual consistency for recommendations. The interview point is naming the trade-off per dataset and what breaks if you choose wrong.

title: Comparing rate limiting algorithms
question: Compare token bucket and leaky bucket rate limiting. When would you choose each?
shortAnswer: Token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity and bounds the long-run rate; leaky bucket smooths bursts into a fixed rate but queueing adds latency. Choose token bucket for bursty legitimate traffic, leaky bucket for a downstream that needs a steady rate.
detailedAnswer: Both bound the rate, but they treat bursts differently. A token bucket holds up to N tokens, refills at a fixed rate, and serves a request immediately if a token is available — so a user opening an app and firing ten requests at once is served, while the long-run rate stays bounded. A leaky bucket queues requests and drains them at a fixed rate, so bursts wait instead of being served, adding latency but giving the downstream system a perfectly smooth load. A fixed-window counter is simpler but allows double the rate across a window boundary; a sliding window counter fixes that with one counter per window. A distributed limiter needs shared state, usually Redis, or each instance enforces its own limit.

title: Parent delegation in class loading
question: Why can two classes with the same name be different types in one JVM?
shortAnswer: Because class identity is the name plus the defining classloader, and parent delegation means each loader asks its parent first — so two loaders can each define their own copy.
detailedAnswer: Classes are loaded on demand by a hierarchy of loaders (bootstrap, platform, application, custom), and each loader asks its parent first before loading a class itself. That is why application code cannot shadow java.lang.String. A class is identified by its name plus the loader that defined it, so the same class loaded by two different loaders — for example, two web applications each loading their own copy of a library — is two different types, and casting between them throws ClassCastException even though the names match. The fix is to share the class through a common parent loader or communicate through an interface loaded by that parent.

title: OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
question: Your service throws OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. What do you check?
shortAnswer: Class metadata, not the heap: classloader leaks (static references, ThreadLocal values, registered drivers keeping a loader alive) or unbounded class generation. Raising -Xmx does not help.
detailedAnswer: Metaspace holds class metadata, and it fills for two reasons: loaders that cannot be collected, or classes generated without bound (dynamic proxies, generated bytecode). A classloader leak usually means something reachable from a GC root — a static map, a ThreadLocal, a JDBC driver registered in a shared registry — still references classes from a loader that should have been collected, for example on web-app redeploy. The diagnosis is a heap dump and a dominator-tree search for the loader and its classes, not a bigger heap: -Xmx sizes the Java heap, and Metaspace is a separate area.

title: MVCC and isolation
question: How does MVCC let readers and writers run at the same time?
shortAnswer: Each row exists in several versions stamped by transaction; a reader sees the version committed when its transaction (or statement) started, so it never blocks on a writer — old versions are later reclaimed.
detailedAnswer: Most modern databases implement isolation with multi-version concurrency control rather than locking every row a transaction reads. Each row has several versions, and a transaction sees the version that was committed when it started (or, under READ COMMITTED, when the statement started). Readers never block writers and writers never block readers, which is why a long REPEATABLE READ transaction can read consistent data while other transactions update the same rows. The cost is garbage: old versions accumulate until no transaction can see them, then PostgreSQL's VACUUM or InnoDB's purge reclaims them. The mechanism also explains why databases differ at the edges — PostgreSQL uses a fixed snapshot, InnoDB uses next-key locks — even at the same isolation level.
